stem: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram, with its vertices named in order round it. $O$ is a point on the side $PQ$ such that $PS=OS$ and $QO=QR$. $P\hat{S}R={=z}^{\circ}$. Calculate the size of $S\hat{O}R$ in degrees.
solution: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\hat{Q}=P\hat{S}R={=z}^{\circ}$.

Since $QO=QR$, $Q\hat{O}R=Q\hat{R}O$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides). Let $Q\hat{O}R=x^{\circ}$. In $\triangle QOR$: $x^{\circ}+x^{\circ}+{=z}^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$), so $x={=t}$.
$P$, $O$ and $Q$ lie on a straight line, so $S\hat{O}R=180^{\circ}-S\hat{O}P-Q\hat{O}R$ (sum of $\angle$s on a str line) $=180^{\circ}-{=180 - z}^{\circ}-{=t}^{\circ}={=180 - 3 * t}^{\circ}$.
notes: Advanced: the book's own configuration (ex7-3-1c, page 254: O on PQ, PS=OS, QO=QR) run in the harder direction. The student is given the angle at S (not the angle SOR) and must chain: opposite angles of a parallelogram, isosceles triangle QOR, co-interior angles at P and S, isosceles triangle POS, angles on a straight line. That is five reasons against the book's three. The book diagram is replaced by wording ('O is a point on the side PQ', vertices in order), so no figure is needed. Geometry verified by coordinates for t = 12, 20, 28, 30, 38: with PS=OS=QO=QR=a the configuration exists for every P=2t<90, and SOR=180-3t, QOR=t, PSR=180-2t each time. The book instance (t=28, PSR=124, SOR=96) is a member of the family. Range t 12..38 keeps P acute (24 to 76 degrees) and PSR obtuse (104 to 156 degrees), as in the book's figure. ex7-8-33c (mid-point theorem) was not used: it needs the mid-point theorem, which is another objective's method.
